slides.text: As the projectionist at the Hayden Planetarium, I always noticed the woman in Row G, Seat 14. Every Wednesday at the 2:00 PM matinee, she walked in wearing hospital scrubs under a wool coat, sat down beneath the dome, and fell fast asleep the second I dimmed the lights. While sixty schoolchildren gasped at the rings of Saturn, Dr. Elena Ross finally got forty-five minutes of peace.

After the third week, I started quietly adjusting the show just for her. I lowered the narrator’s volume by three decibels, lingered an extra four minutes on the soft indigo glow of the Horsehead Nebula, and kept the house lights dim after the crowd filed out so she wouldn't wake with a start. Once, I left a warm paper cup of peppermint tea on the armrest beside her.

On a rainy November afternoon, the auditorium emptied out, but Elena wasn't sleeping. She was looking straight up at my projection booth window, holding two cups of peppermint tea. When I walked down to Row G, she patted Seat 13. 'I’ve spent twelve hours in trauma surgery,' she smiled softly, 'and I just wanted to meet the man who keeps halting the rotation of the universe so I can rest.'
